section_1.title: Intuitive Hook: The 'Moving Window' Concept
section_1.content: Define convolution as a sliding transformation. Introduce the 'Kernel' (filter) as a small, weighted mask that scans across an input grid to produce a new output value.
section_1.example: Imagine a 3x3 'blurring' filter moving across a photo of a cute Golden Retriever; each position calculates the average intensity of the surrounding pixels to soften the edges.

section_2.title: Mathematical Mechanics: The Dot Product Flip
section_2.content: Explain the step-by-step process: Flip the kernel (mathematical convention), overlay it on the input, perform element-wise multiplication, and sum the results. Visual aid: A 2D grid animation showing the overlapping summation.
section_2.example: Representing a signal as a 1D sequence [1, 2, 3] and a kernel [0.5, 0.5]; slide the kernel across to see how the 'weighted moving average' transforms the signal.

section_3.title: Prerequisite Alignment: Why we use Convolutions
section_3.content: Briefly connect convolution to Linear Time-Invariant (LTI) systems. Explain that it captures the 'memory' of a system—how an output is affected by a sequence of historical inputs.
section_3.example: A robotic arm (system) receiving a stream of velocity commands; the convolution determines the arm's precise current position based on the history of all previous movements.

section_4.title: Real-World Application: Feature Extraction
section_4.content: Show how different kernels extract specific features. Edge detection kernels highlight transitions (high contrast), while smoothing kernels reduce noise.
section_4.example: A security camera system using a 'Sobel filter' kernel to instantly detect the sharp edges of an intruder moving in the dark.

section_5.title: Summary & Conclusion
section_5.content: Recap the 'Sliding, Multiplying, Summing' workflow. Emphasize that convolution is the backbone of modern Deep Learning (CNNs) and digital signal processing.
section_5.example: Final visual: A composite graphic showing a raw image input, a kernel transformation, and the final feature map output—'From pixels to intelligence'.

from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text("- " + line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 1.5 + j * 0.8
                y = 2.2 - i * 0.8
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

        self.play(kernel_window.animate.shift(RIGHT*1.4), run_time=2)
        self.remove(kernel_highlight)
